what: Ollie’s Bargain Outlet sells closeout merchandise. It buys surplus inventory, cancelled orders and discontinued goods from manufacturers and other retailers at large discounts, then sells them in no-frills stores at prices well below normal retail. What it stocks changes constantly, because it depends on what it can buy.
customers: Price-conscious shoppers across the eastern and midwestern United States, who come because the inventory changes and the prices are genuinely low.
money: Closeout goods across housewares, food, books, toys, flooring, health and beauty and seasonal categories, through about 600 stores.
moat: The advantage is being the buyer manufacturers call first when they need to clear inventory quickly and quietly, without disrupting their regular retail pricing. That requires scale, cash, and a reputation for taking the whole lot without renegotiating — relationships built over decades. The stores are deliberately cheap to fit out, so new ones pay back quickly.
risks: The shares trade at about 21.1 times earnings, 16.1 times EV/EBITDA and 25.1 times free cash flow, a full price for a retailer.
The business depends on an abundant supply of closeout merchandise, which is more plentiful when other retailers are struggling and scarcer when supply chains are tight.
Growth comes from opening stores, and store expansion eventually runs into geographic limits and self-cannibalisation.
Comparable sales are inherently volatile because the merchandise mix is never the same twice.
Fifteen analysts average a $104.53 target, about 11% above the current price.
opportunities: Revenue has grown strongly, from $1.8B in 2022 to $2.6B in 2026, mostly through new stores.
A net margin of 9.1% is high for discount retail and reflects buying merchandise genuinely cheaply rather than discounting it later.
Debt of $685.9M against $259.7M of cash is manageable, and much of it is lease related.
The closeout model is countercyclical in supply: when other retailers are in trouble, Ollie’s merchandise gets cheaper.
Low-cost store fit-outs mean each new location requires modest capital and pays back quickly.
watch: New store openings and comparable store sales. The growth is almost entirely store count, so the pace of openings and whether existing stores hold their sales are the two things to follow.
view: The closeout model is cleverer than it appears from the shop floor. Ollie’s does not buy merchandise and mark it down; it buys merchandise that is already a problem for somebody else — a cancelled order, a discontinued line, a packaging change — at a price that lets it sell cheaply and still earn a 9.1% net margin. That margin is the tell: a retailer discounting its way to volume does not earn 9%. Buying well is the entire business.

The moat is relationships rather than anything structural, and it is more durable than that sounds. A manufacturer needing to clear inventory quietly, without disrupting its regular retail pricing, calls a buyer it trusts to take the whole lot, pay promptly and not come back to renegotiate. Being on that short list takes decades and scale. It is also why the supply side is countercyclical in a useful way: when other retailers are struggling, closeout merchandise becomes more plentiful and cheaper.

The growth is almost entirely store openings — revenue from $1.8 billion to $2.6 billion over four years, with store count driving most of it — and the economics of each opening are genuinely good because the fit-outs are deliberately basic and pay back quickly. That is a repeatable formula with real runway in the eastern and midwestern United States, and the recent distress at other discount chains has freed up locations.

What stops me from being enthusiastic is the price. At 21.1 times earnings and 25 times free cash flow, the market is paying a growth multiple for a retailer whose growth depends on continuing to open stores at this pace, and store-expansion stories have a known ending: the geography fills up, new stores cannibalise old ones, and comparable sales become the only lever. Comparable sales here are also inherently noisy, because the merchandise is never the same twice. The business is good and the price assumes nothing goes wrong for several years.
bull: Store openings continue at pace with quick paybacks while distress at rival discounters supplies cheaper merchandise, and 9% margins hold on genuinely good buying.
bear: Store expansion runs into geographic limits and cannibalisation, closeout supply tightens, and a 21 times earnings multiple on a retailer contracts hard.
